content.p: Christa Gail Pike was 18 when she tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in Knoxville, Tennessee, in January 1995. She was sentenced to death the following year and has been on the state's death row ever since, for most of that time as the only woman there. On Wednesday 30 September 2026 Tennessee tried to execute her by lethal injection. Two doses of pentobarbital did not kill her. More than an hour after the procedure began, witnesses could still hear her snoring behind a closed curtain, and an ambulance took her from the prison to a hospital.

Her lawyers said two days later that she was unconscious and breathing with a ventilator. Governor Bill Lee ordered an outside review and postponed the state's one other execution scheduled for the year. The executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center called what happened to her "singular and unparalleled".

Pike and Slemmer were students at the Job Corps centre in Knoxville, a training programme for young people from poor backgrounds. Pike believed that Slemmer was trying to draw the attention of her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, who was 17. On 12 January 1995, according to legal documents filed with the US Supreme Court, Pike, Shipp and a friend, Shadolla Peterson, lured Slemmer to a remote part of the University of Tennessee's agricultural campus. Knoxville police said the three attacked her there. She was slashed, beaten and tortured over a long period, her throat was cut, and her skull was crushed with a piece of asphalt.

A pentagram had been carved into her chest, and a piece of her skull was missing. Fellow students said Pike later boasted about the killing and told one of them she had kept the fragment as a "souvenir". The details set off intense press coverage and talk of the occult. Shipp testified at a later hearing that he was the one who carved the pentagram. Pike told police she had been jealous and "wasn't even thinking". Most accounts give Slemmer's age as 19, though an Associated Press report from 2025 gave it as 18.

Pike and Shipp both confessed. In 1996 Pike was convicted of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder. She was 20 when the judge told her she would die by electrocution, which was then the state's only method, and she sobbed as he said it. At that time she was the youngest woman sent to death row in the modern era of American capital punishment.

Shipp could not face the death penalty because of his age. He was sentenced to life in prison, was denied parole in 2025, and is due for review again toward the end of 2031. Peterson, who acted as a lookout, testified against Pike, pleaded guilty to being an accessory after the fact and received six years of probation. Pike's present lawyers say her trial lawyers could have accepted a prosecution offer of life without parole in return for a guilty plea.

In 2001 Pike tried to strangle another inmate, Patricia Jones, and was convicted of attempted first-degree murder. The Correction Department dates that conviction to August 2001. The Associated Press has dated it to 2004 and said it added 25 years to her sentence.

For all but three of her years in prison Pike was the only woman under sentence of death in Tennessee, and she was held apart from other prisoners for up to 23 hours a day. Her lawyers sued, comparing her conditions to solitary confinement, and a settlement in 2024 gave her a job and some mealtimes in the company of a few other women.

Doctors diagnosed bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder only after she was imprisoned. A 226-page clemency petition described a childhood of violence, neglect and sexual abuse, including rapes at 11 and 17, and argued that her mother's heavy drinking during pregnancy had damaged her brain development. Bethany Brand, a psychologist who assessed her for the defence, wrote that the trauma was "almost impossible to grasp because it is so severe". None of this history reached the jury that sentenced her.

One appeals judge put her unease on the record. In a 2018 appeal that Pike lost, US Circuit Judge Jane Stranch wrote that in sentencing her to death "we rule out the possibility that her crime was a product of the immature mind of youth rather than fixed depravity". Pike herself wrote in the petition: "It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I'd done." The victim's mother, May Martinez, publicly backed the execution.

The Tennessee Supreme Court set Pike's execution date a year in advance. On 8 January 2026 her lawyers sued in Davidson County Chancery Court, arguing that a blood disorder made lethal injection unconstitutionally cruel in her case. Her lawyers have identified the condition as thrombocytosis and said that her veins are difficult to access.

Lee denied clemency two days before the execution. On the morning itself, an hour before the scheduled start at 10 a.m., the US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit ordered a short pause to consider a claim that her trial lawyers had failed to present her childhood abuse. The US Supreme Court lifted that stay hours later. Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.

Media witnesses said the curtains of the death chamber at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution were raised at 7:27 p.m., showing Pike strapped to a gurney. "I'm going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life, and that is in love," she said.

She stayed conscious after the first dose. Steven Hale of the Nashville Banner saw her lift her head at 7:54 p.m. Tori Gessner of WKRN saw her point at her arm and ask, "Does this happen like that?" Kim Chandler of the Associated Press said Pike's mouth fell open and she began to snore loudly. The curtains were closed, reopened and closed again. By 8:26 p.m., witnesses reported, a second dose had been given. When the microphone was cut at 8:53 p.m. and the witnesses were told to leave, Chandler said, Pike could still be heard "loudly snoring, clearly very alive". Her lawyers filed emergency motions in three courts while this was happening.

Spivey said the team had spent more than an hour trying to place an intravenous line. By his count at least seven needles went into her left arm, and one looked bent when it came out. The Department of Correction said it had "followed every step of the state's lawful, established execution protocol", and that the protocol allowed nothing beyond what was done. The protocol provides for a second set of syringes if the prisoner is still alive after the first. It does not say what should follow a second failure.

In a court filing two days later, Pike's lawyers said she was unconscious, intubated and on a ventilator in a Nashville-area hospital, where staff were trying to clear the drug from her body. Both arms were "swollen, burned, and blistered" when she arrived. The lawyers believe the lines were wrongly placed or her veins had burst, so that the pentobarbital went into the tissue of her arms. They asked a state court to order all evidence preserved. Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist retained by the defence, told the BBC that a brain injury was "very possible".
Martinez, who had travelled to Nashville to watch, called the night a mess. "I didn't get justice for my daughter," she said.
content.h2: Tennessee's record and what comes next
content.p: It was the state's second failed execution of the year. On 21 May 2026 officials abandoned the execution of Tony Carruthers after failing for over an hour to find a suitable vein. In 2022 Lee had halted the execution of Oscar Smith and paused all executions after admitting that lethal injection drugs had not been properly tested. The state later dropped its three-drug method for pentobarbital alone.

Lee called the failure "deeply disturbing" and ordered "a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred". Pike's lawyers want her sentence commuted. Spivey said she "has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty". Senator Marsha Blackburn called for a return to the electric chair, and the United Nations human rights chief, Volker Türk, urged the state not to try again.

The law on a second attempt is thin. Austin Sarat of Amherst College pointed to Willie Francis, who survived a faulty electric chair in Louisiana and was executed after the Supreme Court rejected his appeal, and to Romell Broom, whose Ohio execution was abandoned in 2009 when no vein could be found. Pike's case is different, Sarat said, because the lethal drugs actually entered her system. Tennessee officials have not said whether they will try again.
